```bash
    viz: Option<&crate::viz::VizSender>,
    model: &str,
    ref_idx: usize,
    kind_name: &str,
    kind: Kind,
) -> bool {
    let member: HashSet<usize> = faces.iter().copied().collect();
    let vstar = vertex_star_map(mesh, faces);
    let n_sample = config.viz_seed_samples.max(1);
    let stride = (faces.len() / n_sample).max(1);
    let anchors: Vec<usize> = faces.iter().copied().step_by(stride).take(n_sample).collect();
    let show = config.viz_seed_show.as_str();

    for a in anchors {
        let out = probe_anchor::<S>(
            mesh, in_region, &member, &vstar, truth, centroids, config, kind, a,
        );
        let facet_ok = out.winner.is_some();
        let wanted = match show {
            "all" => true,
            "covering" => facet_ok,
            _ => !facet_ok,
        };
        if !wanted {
            continue;
        }
        if out.attempts.is_empty() {
            let status = format!(
                "{model} ref#{ref_idx} {kind_name} ({} facets) | facet {a} | NO CONFORMING SEED \
                 SET EXISTS containing this facet under the section's rule for a {kind_name}",
                faces.len()
            );
            if !emit(viz, mesh, None, truth, &status) {
                return false;
            }
            continue;
        }
        for (i, case) in out.cases.iter().enumerate() {
            let verdict = if facet_ok && i == out.cases.len() - 1 {
                "FACET OK — this seed set covers".to_string()
            } else if facet_ok {
                case.why(truth.len())
            } else {
                format!("FACET FAILS ({}/{} attempts) — {}", i + 1, out.attempts.len(), case.why(truth.len()))
            };
            let seed_worst = case
                .seed_verdicts
                .iter()
                .map(|(_, v)| v.vratio)
                .fold(0.0_f64, f64::max);
            let status = format!(
                "{model} ref#{ref_idx} {kind_name} ({} facets) | facet {a} | seed {} x{} | \
                 own fit: vertex {:.2}x vtol{} | {verdict}",
                faces.len(),
                case.shape,
                case.seed.len(),
                seed_worst,
                if case.seed_verdicts.is_empty() {
                    ", no fit exists".to_string()
                } else if case.self_ok {
                    String::new()
                } else {
                    format!(", ADMISSION FAILS on {}", dominant_cause(&case.seed_verdicts))
                },
            );
            if !emit(viz, mesh, Some((a, case)), truth, &status) {
                return false;
            }
        }
    }
    true
}

/// Draw one step (or print it, headless). Returns false when the user quits.
fn emit(
    viz: Option<&crate::viz::VizSender>,
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    case: Option<(usize, &SeedCase)>,
    truth: &HashSet<usize>,
    status: &str,
) -> bool {
    let Some(viz) = viz else {
        eprintln!("  [seed] {status}");
        return true;
    };
    let mut ov = crate::viz::VizOverlay::new();
    let anchor = match case {
        Some((a, c)) => {
            let blocked_only: Vec<usize> = c
                .blocked
                .iter()
                .filter(|(_, v)| !v.ok())
                .map(|&(f, _)| f)
                .collect();
            let covered: Vec<usize> = c
                .result
                .iter()
                .copied()
                .filter(|f| truth.contains(f) && !c.seed.contains(f))
                .collect();
            let missed_only: Vec<usize> = c
                .missed
                .iter()
                .copied()
                .filter(|f| !blocked_only.contains(f))
                .collect();
            for (idxs, color) in [
                (covered, C_COVERED),
                (c.overshoot.clone(), C_OVERSHOOT),
                (missed_only, C_MISSED),
                (blocked_only, C_BLOCKED),
                (c.seed.clone(), C_SEED),
                (vec![a], C_ANCHOR),
            ] {
                if !idxs.is_empty() {
                    ov.face_highlights.push(crate::viz::FaceHighlight {
                        face_indices: idxs,
                        color,
                    });
                }
            }
            a
        }
        None => *truth.iter().next().unwrap_or(&0),
    };
    let c = face_centroid(&mesh.faces[anchor], &mesh.vertices);
    ov.focus_point = Some([c[0] as f32, c[1] as f32, c[2] as f32]);
    let n = facet_normal(mesh, anchor);
    ov.focus_normal = Some([n[0] as f32, n[1] as f32, n[2] as f32]);
    ov.status_text = status.to_string();
    !matches!(viz.show_and_wait(ov), crate::viz::VizAction::Quit)
}
```

```bash
fn diagnose<S: SurfaceType>(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    in_region: &[bool],
    seed: &[usize],
    truth: &HashSet<usize>,
    centroids: &[[f64; 3]],
    config: &Config,
    shape: &'static str,
) -> SeedCase {
    let vtol = config.vertex_tolerance_mm;
    let stol = config.surface_tolerance_mm;
    let (mut verdict, result, rounds, self_ok, fit) =
        grow_clean::<S>(mesh, in_region, seed, centroids, config);
    if verdict == Basin::Exact {
        verdict = classify(&result, truth);
    }
    let rset: HashSet<usize> = result.iter().copied().collect();
    let mut missed: Vec<usize> = truth.difference(&rset).copied().collect();
    let mut overshoot: Vec<usize> = rset.difference(truth).copied().collect();
    missed.sort_unstable();
    overshoot.sort_unstable();

    // Split the missed facets by CAUSE: refused by validation at the frontier,
    // not mesh-reachable, or cut into a different smooth region by stage 2.1
    // (in which case no seed can reach them at all).
    let mut blocked: Vec<(usize, FacetVerdict)> = Vec::new();
    let mut unreachable: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
    let mut outside_region: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
    for &m in &missed {
        if !in_region[m] {
            outside_region.push(m);
            continue;
        }
        let vc = mesh.faces[m].vertex_count as usize;
        let touches = mesh.faces[m].neighbors[..vc]
            .iter()
            .any(|&ni| ni >= 0 && rset.contains(&(ni as usize)));
        match (touches, fit.as_ref()) {
            (true, Some(f)) => {
                blocked.push((m, facet_verdict::<S>(mesh, m, f, centroids, vtol, stol)))
            }
            (true, None) => {}
            (false, _) => unreachable.push(m),
        }
    }

    // Every seed facet against the seed set's OWN first fit — the admission
    // quantity, clause by clause.
    let verts = vertices_of(mesh, seed);
    let mut seed_verdicts: Vec<(usize, FacetVerdict)> = Vec::new();
    if let Some(mut f0) = S::fit_surface(mesh, seed, &verts, 0) {
        S::determine_convexity(mesh, seed, &mut f0);

            seed_verdicts.push((fi, facet_verdict::<S>(mesh, fi, &f0, centroids, vtol, stol)));
        }
    }

    SeedCase {
        shape,
        seed: seed.to_vec(),
        verdict,
        result,
        rounds,
        self_ok,
        missed,
        overshoot,
        blocked,
        unreachable,
        outside_region,
        truth_connected: {
            let mut t: Vec<usize> = truth.iter().copied().collect();
            t.sort_unstable();
            is_connected(mesh, &t)
        },
        seed_verdicts,
    }
}
```

> Generating results table... Cone facets are the real problem—22% have no valid seed at any size up to 48, which suggests cones are fundamentally different from the other shapes. The sample is thin though (488 anchors across 41 faces, and the reference cone is just 59 planes), so I should note that limitation. For torus, the vertex star alone works 40% of the time, expanding to neighboring vertex stars gets another 25%, and the remaining facets need seeds of 8–48 vertices.
> 
> The stopping condition is driven by the admission predicate, not a fixed count. The key insight for why a star works better than a chain: on a torus, the normal lines cross the axis at a point that shifts with the tube angle, so a seed locked to one tube angle can't determine the axis—a two-quad chain along the major direction is exactly underdetermined. A star wraps around a grid node and spans both directions by construction, which is why it's the right choice.
> 
> Now I'm setting up the visualization to iterate through anchor facets and highlight only those where every conforming seed fails, using cone models like `simple_cone`, `cone_cylinder`, and `nosecone` to show the high failure rate, plus a torus model like `filleted_hole_block`.

All three corrections applied. The window is open on `filleted_hole_block`, paused on a torus facet whose vertex-star seed fails.

## What changed

**The visualization now walks anchor facets, not seed sets.** For each facet it builds every conforming seed set *containing* that facet, grows each, and stops only when *all* of them fail — which is your invariant. Colours: **white** the anchor facet · **green** the rest of the seed · **blue** covered · **red** overshoot · **orange** true facets that blocked growth · **yellow** missed otherwise. The status line reads `facet N | seed <shape> xK | FACET FAILS (i/M attempts) — <diagnosis>`.

**Seed sets are connected again** — the disconnected `split` and `random` shapes are gone. The generators are now the DEVELOPMENT_PLAN rules read literally: plane = the facet; cylinder = a connected 6-vertex chain ≤ 4 facets; cone = that, or three triangles sharing a vertex; sphere = the facet plus its edge neighbours (and the same ring about each neighbour).

**The sharp-edge partition is disabled for growth**, so `partition-cut` can no longer occur. `--viz-seed-confine-region` restores it if you want to see that effect.

## Torus rule

Your instinct is right about the shape and the reason is identifiability, not taste. A torus's normal lines cross the axis at a point that *slides with the tube angle*, so a seed confined to one tube angle cannot pin the axis — and two quads along the major direction is exactly that, which is why you spotted it as underdetermined. A vertex star wraps a grid node, so it spans both parametric directions by construction.

But one star is not enough for 7 DOF. Measured, the least support that works per torus facet:

| star | +star2 | +ball8 | +ball12 | +ball16 | +ball24 | +ball32 | +ball48 | never |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 40% | 65% | 74% | 87% | 91% | 94% | 99% | 99.2% | 0.8% |

So the rule I'd propose:

> **Torus:** the closed ring of facets about one vertex (its vertex star), grown outward while the seed set's own fit does not yet validate every facet of the seed set. Typically 4–12 facets, occasionally up to 32.

The stopping condition is the admission predicate, not a count — which is the same predicate that terminates growth, one scale down. Requiring the ring to *close* matters: complete stars win 40% of facets, cut ones 4%.

## The success table at your seed sizes

10 173 anchor facets, 897 reference faces, 107 models. Chains capped at 4 facets, partition disabled.

| type | anchors | **your rule alone** | + grown ball | faces all-OK (your rule) | (grown) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sphere | 1 644 | **100.0%** | 100.0% | **100.0%** | 100.0% |
| plane | 1 740 | **99.9%** | 100.0% | 98.7% | 100.0% |
| cylinder | 4 801 | **94.1%** | 99.5% | 86.4% | 99.5% |
| torus | 1 500 | 65.4% | **99.2%** | 22.4% | 99.2% |
| cone | 488 | 49.4% | 77.7% | 26.8% | 75.6% |
| **all** | 10 173 | **89.7%** | **98.6%** | | |

Restating the invariant existentially is worth a lot: the universal reading gave 80.6% of facets and 34.9% of surfaces; this gives **89.7%** on your rules as written and **98.6%** with the growth fallback.

**Your sphere rule is exactly right — 100.0% of facets, 100.0% of faces, no exceptions.** Your plane rule likewise. Your cylinder chain suffices for 94% of facets on its own.

Which rule suffices, per facet:

- **plane**: `facet` 100%
- **sphere**: `edge-ring` 100%
- **cylinder**: `chain6` 94%, ball8 5%, ball12 1%
- **torus**: `star` 40%, `star2` 21%, `star2-cut` 4%, balls 8–48 for 34%, never 1%
- **cone**: `chain6` 28%, `apex3` 21%, balls for 27%, **never 22%**

Your `apex3` alternative for cones earns its place — it is the *least* working rule for 21% of cone facets, cases `chain6` cannot reach.

## Cone is the remaining gap

22% of cone facets have no working conforming seed at any size up to 48 facets. Causes: no fit exists 51%, the seed's own fit refuses its own facets 38%, stalled 11%. That is consistent with everything measured earlier — a cone needs far more support than any other type, and it's the one place where "grow the seed until it's admissible" doesn't rescue it. Caveat: cone n = 488 anchors over 41 faces is the thinnest sample in the table, partly because `cone_15x20.step` is a faceted reference and contributes no cone faces.

> The key insight is that vtol = 5e-5 mm, so 193.5× vtol is about 9.7e-3 mm — and the fact that *every* facet is off by a similar magnitude suggests this isn't a random outlier but a systematic miss, meaning the fitter either didn't converge properly or converged to an entirely different surface than the data actually lies on.
> 
> I'm considering two main culprits: either the torus fitter's initialization and Levenberg-Marquardt solver are failing to converge on 9 facets spanning only ~2 steps in each direction (hitting a poor local minimum or iteration cap), or the distance function itself is measuring to the wrong branch of the torus — like computing distance to the inner tube when the facets are actually on the outer tube, or vice versa.

The fact that it doesn't means the optimizer failed, not the model. So I need to verify empirically by comparing the fitted torus parameters (R, r, axis, center) against the reference to see where things went wrong.

```bash
cd .; python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='src/stage2/invariants.rs'
s=open(p).read()
anchor = "/// Grow one seed set and work out, in detail, what happened to it."
new = r'''/// Why did a seed set's own fit refuse its own facets?
///
/// The question this answers is whether the failure is a shortage of
/// *information* or a failure of the *fitter*: it prints the residual the
/// reference's own exact parameters achieve on the very same facets — the floor
/// any fit of that type could reach — beside the residual the fitter actually
/// achieved, and the two parameter sets side by side. Gated by
/// `BREPPER_INV_FITDUMP=1`.
fn fit_dump(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    seed: &[usize],
    ref_surf: &RefSurface,
    kind: Kind,
    vtol: f64,
    quantum: f64,
    label: &str,
) {
    let verts = vertices_of(mesh, seed);
    let truth_max = verts
        .iter()
        .filter_map(|&v| ref_distance(ref_surf, vertex_pos(mesh, v)))
        .fold(0.0_f64, f64::max);
    eprintln!(
        "  [fit] {label}: {} facets, {} vertices | the REFERENCE's own parameters fit these \
         vertices to {:.3e} mm = {:.2}x vtol = {:.2} quanta",
        seed.len(),
        verts.len(),
        truth_max,
        truth_max / vtol,
        truth_max / quantum,
    );
    match kind {
        Kind::Torus => {
            let RefSurface::Torus {
                centre,
                axis_dir,
                major,
                minor,
            } = *ref_surf
            else {
                return;
            };
            match ToroidalSurface::fit_surface(mesh, seed, &verts, 0) {
                Some(f) => {
                    let fitted_max = verts
                        .iter()
                        .map(|&v| ToroidalSurface::vertex_distance(&f, &vertex_pos(mesh, v)))
                        .fold(0.0_f64, f64::max);
                    let d = unit(axis_dir);
                    let fd = unit(f.axis_direction);
                    let axis_err = norm([
                        fd[1] * d[2] - fd[2] * d[1],
                        fd[2] * d[0] - fd[0] * d[2],
                        fd[0] * d[1] - fd[1] * d[0],
                    ])
                    .clamp(0.0, 1.0)
                    .asin()
                    .to_degrees();
                    eprintln!(
                        "  [fit]   truth: R {major:.6} r {minor:.6} centre ({:.4},{:.4},{:.4})",
                        centre[0], centre[1], centre[2]
                    );
                    eprintln!(
                        "  [fit]   fitted: R {:.6} r {:.6} centre ({:.4},{:.4},{:.4})  \
                         axis off by {axis_err:.4}deg  -> residual {:.3e} mm = {:.1}x vtol",
                        f.major_radius,
                        f.minor_radius,
                        f.center[0],
                        f.center[1],
                        f.center[2],
                        fitted_max,
                        fitted_max / vtol,
                    );
                    eprintln!(
                        "  [fit]   R error {:+.4} mm ({:+.1}%), r error {:+.6} mm ({:+.2}%)",
                        f.major_radius - major,
                        100.0 * (f.major_radius - major) / major.max(1e-30),
                        f.minor_radius - minor,
                        100.0 * (f.minor_radius - minor) / minor.max(1e-30),
                    );
                }
                None => eprintln!("  [fit]   fitted: none (fit_torus declined)"),
            }
        }
        Kind::Cylinder | Kind::Cone => {
            if let Some(f) = ConicalSurface::fit_surface(mesh, seed, &verts, 0) {
                let fitted_max = verts
                    .iter()
                    .map(|&v| ConicalSurface::vertex_distance(&f, &vertex_pos(mesh, v)))
                    .fold(0.0_f64, f64::max);
                eprintln!(
                    "  [fit]   fitted: half-angle {:.4}deg radius {:.6} -> residual {:.3e} mm \
                     = {:.1}x vtol",
                    f.half_angle.to_degrees(),
                    f.radius,
                    fitted_max,
                    fitted_max / vtol,
                );
            }
        }
        Kind::Sphere => {
            if let Some(f) = SphericalSurface::fit_surface(mesh, seed, &verts, 0) {
                let fitted_max = verts
                    .iter()
                    .map(|&v| SphericalSurface::vertex_distance(&f, &vertex_pos(mesh, v)))
                    .fold(0.0_f64, f64::max);
                eprintln!(
                    "  [fit]   fitted: r {:.6} -> residual {:.3e} mm = {:.1}x vtol",
                    f.radius,
                    fitted_max,
                    fitted_max / vtol
                );
            }
        }
        _ => {}
    }
}

/// Grow one seed set and work out, in detail, what happened to it.'''
assert s.count(anchor)==1
s=s.replace(anchor,new,1)

# thread the reference surface + kind into diagnose so the dump can fire
s=s.replace("""    config: &Config,
    shape: &'static str,
) -> SeedCase {
    let vtol = config.vertex_tolerance_mm;""",
"""    config: &Config,
    shape: &'static str,
    ref_surf: Option<(&RefSurface, Kind, f64, &str)>,
) -> SeedCase {
    let vtol = config.vertex_tolerance_mm;""")
s=s.replace("""    SeedCase {
        shape,
        seed: seed.to_vec(),""",
"""    if let Some((rs, kind, quantum, label)) = ref_surf {
        if !self_ok && std::env::var("BREPPER_INV_FITDUMP").is_ok() {
            fit_dump(mesh, seed, rs, kind, vtol, quantum, label);
        }
    }

    SeedCase {
        shape,
        seed: seed.to_vec(),""")
open(p,'w').write(s)
```

```
pub(crate) fn torus(faces: &[usize], mesh: &ConnectedMesh) -> Option<Initial> {
    let (pos, dir) = axis_line_from_normals(faces, mesh)?;
    let profile = profile_coords(faces, mesh, pos, dir);
    if profile.len() < 3 {
        return None;
    }
    let ((major, z0), minor) = super::toroidal::fit_circle_2d(&profile)?;
    if !(major > 0.0 && minor > 0.0 && minor < major) {
        return None;
    }
    let centre = [
        pos[0] + dir[0] * z0,
        pos[1] + dir[1] * z0,
        pos[2] + dir[2] * z0,
    ];
    Some(Initial::Torus {
        centre,
        axis_dir: dir,
        major,
        minor,
    })
}
```

So the global minimum sits at the true parameters by six to nine orders of magnitude. This is not an identifiability problem, not a tolerance problem, and not a shortage of support. **It is the least-squares torus fit converging into the wrong basin.**

## The wrong basin has a geometric identity

Look at the fitted numbers again: R = 20.745, r = 18.745, so **R − r = 2.0004** against a true minor radius of **2.0000**.

That is the fitter presenting its **inner equator** to the patch. At a torus's inner equator the two principal curvatures are `+1/r` along the meridian and `−1/(R−r)` along the parallel — a saddle. By setting `R − r = 2`, the fit matches the fillet's tube curvature `1/2` with the *wrong principal direction*, which forces its axis a quarter-turn round. Hence 89.86°.

Across 215 rejected torus fits on four fillet models:

- median fitted axis error **72.4°**; **39%** land within 5° of perpendicular
- **30%** have `R − r` within 15% of the true minor radius
- the fitted R ranges **0.03 to 66.22 mm** on fillets whose true R is 1–9 mm

So the axis-swapped saddle is the dominant wrong basin but not the only one — there are also collapsed fits (R = 1.51, r = 0.64) and runaway ones (R = 37.8). What they share is that R is nearly free: moving `(R, r) → (R + t, r + t)` preserves the inner-equator radius and barely changes the surface there, so once the optimizer is in that valley it slides along it and stops wherever. That is why `R − r` is pinned to 0.02% while R varies by a factor of 2000.

Worth noting: the patch sweeps **34.7°** about the fitted axis, well clear of `MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG`'s 20°, so this is *not* the small-sweep degeneracy the codebase already guards. It's a distinct failure.

## Phase 1.1's closed form does not rescue it

Since that initializer was built, unit-tested to 1e-6, and never wired in, it was the obvious candidate. On these same seeds it gets the axis closer in kind (7.6–16.5° off rather than 88–90°) but r badly wrong — **0.34–0.54 against 2.0** — for a residual of 6 200–9 965× vtol. Its `fit_circle_2d` profile step is the weak part on a short tube arc. So wiring it in as-is would not fix this.

## What this means for the numbers I reported

**The torus rows throughout have been measuring `fit_torus`'s convergence, not your seed rule.** The 65.4% for the vertex star, and the 39.9% before I widened it, are not statements about how much information a star carries — a star carries enough, as the 2.08-quanta truth residual proves. They are statements about how often the optimizer finds the minimum from a small patch. Read the earlier torus figures that way.

It also explains why growing the seed to 8–48 facets lifted tori to 99.2%: a patch spanning more of the tube can no longer be mimicked by an inner equator, so the wrong basin stops existing. Growth was papering over a fitter defect, not supplying missing information.

## Two leads, neither measured

The `R − r ≈ patch tube radius` plus near-perpendicular axis signature is cheap to detect, and on a *convex* fillet a saddle fit should already fail the orientation clause — some of these did report `2 on ORIENTATION`, so that check is catching it only partly. Seeding `r` from the patch's own dominant principal curvature (which the jet already provides) rather than letting it float would remove the valley's entrance. Either would be a change to `fit_torus`, not to the seed requirements — which is the useful conclusion: **the torus problem in the Invariants section is not a seeding question.**

The diagnostic is behind `BREPPER_INV_FITDUMP=1` and prints the truth-vs-fit comparison for any seed set that fails admission, so you can point it at any case the window shows you.

```
fn fit_torus(
    face_indices: &[usize],
    vertex_set: &[usize],
    faces: &[MeshFace],
    vertices: &[MeshVertex],
) -> Option<([f64; 3], [f64; 3], f64, f64)> {
    let max_err = |fit: &([f64; 3], [f64; 3], f64, f64)| -> f64 {
        vertex_set.iter().map(|&vi| {
            vertex_to_torus_distance(&vertices[vi], &fit.0, &fit.1, fit.2, fit.3).abs()
        }).fold(0.0_f64, f64::max)
    };
    // Structural validity must be checked BEFORE picking the lowest-error
    // candidate: on small corner patches the tube-center method can return
    // a self-intersecting fit (minor > major) with a locally lower vertex
    // error, which would shadow a valid rescue fit and then be rejected
    // downstream.
    let valid = |fit: &([f64; 3], [f64; 3], f64, f64)| -> bool {
        fit.2 > 0.0 && fit.3 > 0.0 && fit.3 <= fit.2
    };

    // Try the tube-center and SOR methods and keep the better fit.
    let inner = fit_torus_inner(face_indices, vertex_set, faces, vertices);
    let sor = fit_torus_sor(face_indices, vertex_set, faces, vertices);
    let mut best: Option<(f64, TorusFitTuple)> = None;
    for cand in [inner, sor].into_iter().flatten() {
        if !valid(&cand) {
            continue;
        }
        let err = max_err(&cand);
        if best.as_ref().is_none_or(|(e, _)| err < *e) {
            best = Some((err, cand));
        }
    }

    // Multi-axis rescue for small patches, only when the geometric methods
    // fail to reach CAD-mesh precision (bounds the extra LM cost to the
    // rare hard cases).
    const RESCUE_ERR_THRESHOLD: f64 = 1e-4; // mm
    if best.as_ref().is_none_or(|(e, _)| *e > RESCUE_ERR_THRESHOLD) {
        if let Some(cand) = fit_torus_axes_rescue(face_indices, vertex_set, faces, vertices) {
            if valid(&cand) {
                let err = max_err(&cand);
                if best.as_ref().is_none_or(|(e, _)| err < *e) {
                    best = Some((err, cand));
                }
            }
        }
    }

    best.map(|(_, c)| c)
}

fn fit_torus_inner(
    face_indices: &[usize],
    vertex_set: &[usize],
    faces: &[MeshFace],
    vertices: &[MeshVertex],
) -> Option<([f64; 3], [f64; 3], f64, f64)> {
    if vertex_set.len() < 7 || face_indices.len() < 3 {
        return None;
    }

    // Sort vertices for deterministic iteration order (avoids floating-point
    // accumulation-order differences across runs due to HashSet randomization).
    let sorted_verts: Vec<usize> = {
        let mut v: Vec<usize> = vertex_set.to_vec();
        v.sort_unstable();
        v
    };

    // Step 1: Estimate minor radius from normal-line intersections of adjacent face pairs.
    let mut r_estimates: Vec<f64> = Vec::new();
    let face_set: HashSet<usize> = face_indices.iter().copied().collect();

    for &fi in face_indices {
        let n1 = match faces[fi].normal {
            Some(n) => n,
            None => continue,
        };
        let c1 = face_centroid(&faces[fi], vertices);
        let vc = faces[fi].vertex_count as usize;

        for &ni in &faces[fi].neighbors[..vc] {
            if ni < 0 { continue; }
            let ni = ni as usize;
            if !face_set.contains(&ni) { continue; }
            if ni <= fi { continue; } // avoid duplicates

            let n2 = match faces[ni].normal {
                Some(n) => n,
                None => continue,
            };
            let c2 = face_centroid(&faces[ni], vertices);

            // Normal-line intersection
            if let Some((t, s, dist)) = normal_line_intersection(&c1, &n1, &c2, &n2) {
                // For a torus, both t and s should have the same sign (both pointing
                // toward the tube center) and similar magnitude ≈ minor_radius.
                // The closest-approach distance should be small relative to |t|.
                let t_abs = t.abs();
                let s_abs = s.abs();
                if t_abs < 1e-10 || s_abs < 1e-10 { continue; }

                // t and s should have the same sign for consistent curvature
                if t * s < 0.0 { continue; }

                // The ratio |t|/|s| should be close to 1 for a torus
                let ratio = t_abs / s_abs;
                if !(0.3..=3.0).contains(&ratio) { continue; }

                // The closest-approach distance should be small relative to the radius
                let avg_r = (t_abs + s_abs) / 2.0;
                if dist > avg_r * 0.5 { continue; }

                r_estimates.push(avg_r);
            }
        }
    }
```

```bash
    // percentile instead of median to avoid contamination from azimuthal estimates.
    r_estimates.sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap());
    let minor_r = r_estimates[r_estimates.len() / 4];

    if minor_r < 1e-10 {
        return None;
    }
"""
new_head = """    if r_estimates.is_empty() {
        return None;
    }
    r_estimates.sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap());

    // The adjacent-pair normal-line intersections are a MIXTURE of two
    // populations: tube curvature (≈ r) from edges across the tube, and
    // azimuthal curvature (≈ R ± r) from edges along the major circle. The tube
    // estimates are the smaller ones, and this used to pick the 25th percentile
    // to land in that population.
    //
    // On a large patch that works. On a small one it does not, and the failure
    // is severe rather than marginal: a 4-facet vertex star of a fillet yields
    // only a handful of pairs, so if just one of them is a tube pair the 25th
    // percentile is an AZIMUTHAL estimate — several times too large. Every
    // later step then compounds it: the tube centres are placed at `v + r·n`
    // with the wrong r, so they lie on a circle in the wrong plane,
    // `fit_circle_3d` fits that circle, and LM refines into a basin with the
    // axis a quarter-turn off and the data sitting on the fitted torus's INNER
    // EQUATOR — the fitted `R - r` comes out equal to the true minor radius.
    // Measured on `filleted_hole_block`'s r = 2 fillet: R = 20.7, r = 18.7,
    // axis 89.9° off, residual 193× vertex tolerance, against the reference's
    // own parameters fitting the same 16 vertices to 2.1 float32 quanta. The
    // sum-squared residual at the truth was 1.4e7× smaller, so the global
    // minimum was never in doubt — only the starting point.
    //
    // The fix is not a better percentile, which would be another statistic on a
    // sample of four. It is to stop guessing which population an estimate came
    // from and try several, keeping whichever produces the lowest-residual fit
    // — the same select-the-best-candidate structure `fit_torus` already uses
    // one level up for its inner/SOR/rescue methods. Selection is decisive here
    // because the correct candidate's residual is orders of magnitude better,
    // and it introduces no tolerance: `CANDIDATE_R_MAX` only bounds the work.
    const CANDIDATE_R_MAX: usize = 6;
    let candidates: Vec<f64> = {
        // Spread over the sorted estimates, always including the smallest (the
        // purest tube reading) and the old 25th percentile (so anything that
        // used to work still gets its chance).
        let n = r_estimates.len();
        let mut picks: Vec<f64> = vec![r_estimates[0], r_estimates[n / 4]];
        for k in 1..CANDIDATE_R_MAX {
            picks.push(r_estimates[(k * n) / CANDIDATE_R_MAX]);
        }
        picks.retain(|&r| r >= 1e-10);
        picks.sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap());
        picks.dedup_by(|a, b| (*a - *b).abs() <= 1e-12 * b.abs().max(1.0));
        picks
    };
    if candidates.is_empty() {
        return None;
    }

    let mut best_fit: Option<(f64, ([f64; 3], [f64; 3], f64, f64))> = None;
    for minor_r in candidates {
        if let Some(cand) =
            fit_torus_inner_from_r(minor_r, &sorted_verts, face_indices, faces, vertices)
        {
            if cand.2 <= 0.0 || cand.3 <= 0.0 || cand.3 > cand.2 {
                continue;
            }
            let err = sorted_verts
                .iter()
                .map(|&vi| {
                    vertex_to_torus_distance(&vertices[vi], &cand.0, &cand.1, cand.2, cand.3).abs()
                })
                .fold(0.0_f64, f64::max);
            if best_fit.as_ref().is_none_or(|(e, _)| err < *e) {
                best_fit = Some((err, cand));
            }
        }
    }
    return best_fit.map(|(_, c)| c);
}

/// Steps 2-4 of the tube-centre method for one candidate minor radius: place
/// the tube centres, fit their circle, refine by LM.
fn fit_torus_inner_from_r(
    minor_r: f64,
    sorted_verts: &[usize],
    face_indices: &[usize],
    faces: &[MeshFace],
    vertices: &[MeshVertex],
) -> Option<([f64; 3], [f64; 3], f64, f64)> {
"""
assert s.count(old_head)==1
s=s.replace(old_head,new_head)
open(p,'w').write(s)
```

```bash
/// Levenberg-Marquardt refinement of a torus from a starting guess. Returns
/// `None` when there are too few points or the solve leaves a non-physical
/// radius, in which case the caller keeps its own starting guess.
pub(super) fn refine_torus_lm(
    points: &[[f64; 3]],
    axis: [f64; 3],
    center: [f64; 3],
    major_r: f64,
    minor_r: f64,
) -> Option<([f64; 3], [f64; 3], f64, f64)> {
    if points.len() < 7 {
        return None;
    }
    let problem = TorusLMProblem::new(points.to_vec(), axis, center, major_r, minor_r);
    let (result, _report) = LevenbergMarquardt::new().with_patience(150).minimize(problem);
    let refined_axis = result.axis_dir_from_params(&result.params);
    let refined_center = [result.params[2], result.params[3], result.params[4]];
    let refined_major_r = result.params[5];
    let refined_minor_r = result.params[6];
    (refined_major_r > 0.0 && refined_minor_r > 0.0)
        .then_some((refined_center, refined_axis, refined_major_r, refined_minor_r))
}"""
```

<!-- msg_011Cdm95DmbMuUqyfJEFhVXg -->

I tried both. One works, one is refuted, and I've reverted the fitter so the tree is green — the patch is saved at [tmp/torus-candidate-sweep.patch](tmp/torus-candidate-sweep.patch).

## Root cause confirmed

`fit_torus_inner` estimates the minor radius from normal-line intersections of *adjacent facet pairs*, which mix two populations — tube curvature (≈ r) and azimuthal curvature (≈ R ± r) — and separates them by taking the **25th percentile**, on the reasoning that tube readings are the smaller ones.

On a large patch that works. On a 4–9 facet vertex star there are only a handful of pairs, so if just one is a tube pair the 25th percentile is an *azimuthal* reading, several times too large. Everything downstream compounds it: tube centres get placed at `v + r·n` with the wrong r, so they lie on a circle in the wrong plane, `fit_circle_3d` fits that circle, and LM refines into the basin you saw. It is a statistic on a sample of four.

## Lead 2 — seed r properly: works at seed level

Replacing the percentile with a small candidate sweep over the r estimates, selecting by the resulting fit's residual — the same select-the-best structure `fit_torus` already uses one level up for its inner/SOR/rescue methods. No tolerance introduced; `CANDIDATE_R_MAX = 6` only bounds work.

| torus seed rule, per-facet | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `filleted_hole_block` | 25.0% | **75.0%** |
| `filleted_cylinder` | 54.2% | **75.0%** |
| `filleted_pipe` | 89.6% | **93.8%** |

Corpus cost — 13 of the 14 probe models are byte-identical; one moves:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `stepped_block_toroidal_fillets_fine` | 18/38/0/0/18/1 (75) | 20/38/0/0/18/0 (76) |
| `stepped_block_toroidal_fillets_medium` | 33/31/0/0/19/1 (84) | unchanged |

Suite: **594 passed / 1 failed / 32 ignored** — the failure is `remesh_cone_tangent_fine`, and DEVELOPMENT_PLAN already names that model as the canary for this class of change ("its freeform rung fails as ill-conditioned; if 5a makes freeform stronger, this model is the canary"). A torus that can now be fitted from a small patch wins a competition it used to lose. So it's the canary firing rather than an unexplained break — but it *is* a break, which is why I reverted rather than left it in.

## Lead 1 — the guard/closed-form route: refuted

Wiring in Phase 1.1's closed-form initializer as a second candidate, LM-refined and judged on residual, takes the torus seed rate to **100% on all three models**. It also destroys the decomposition:

| | before | with closed form |
|---|---|---|
| stepped fine | 18/38/0/0/18/1 (75) | **72/37/0/0/18/0 (127)** |
| stepped medium | 33/31/0/0/19/1 (84) | 30/31/0/0/18/1 (80) — loses a torus |

That's the interesting failure. The closed form is *unambiguously the better fit* on the seed — axis 0.049° off against the geometric fit's 89.9°, R = 8.9996 against a true 9 — and it is selected only when its residual is lower. A strictly better-conditioned candidate pool, selected on residual, made the end-to-end result 70% worse.

**Residual on the current support does not predict how a fit will grow.** On a large support the closed form can win the comparison while being the worse surface for the flood that follows, and the plane count then explodes. That's a new instance of a pattern this project has hit from other directions (complexity pricing, the self-calibrating tolerance), and it's the reason I'd treat any "add a better candidate and select by residual" idea here as needing the corpus gate, not just a unit test.

## One methodology note

My first attribution run was wrong and nearly sent me the wrong way. I compared using `brepper --compare --stage 2` while the baseline came from `dump_regions surfaces`, and those two disagree on identical code (126 vs 75 surfaces on stepped fine). The "control" therefore looked like a regression and I briefly blamed the sweep instead of the closed form. Restoring the original file and re-measuring with the same tool settled it. Same lesson as the recorded "verify artifacts, not proxies" — a baseline is only a baseline for the exact invocation that produced it.

## Where this leaves it

The percentile is a genuine defect and the sweep is a genuine fix at seed scale, but it costs one canary test and one surface on the corpus's hardest model. That trade is yours to make, not mine — reapply with:

```bash
git apply tmp/torus-candidate-sweep.patch
```

If you want it landed, the honest next step is diagnosing `remesh_cone_tangent_fine` specifically rather than accepting it, since a torus displacing a cone there is the same super-model pathology `MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG` exists for and may just need that guard to see the new fits.

Current tree: `toroidal.rs` reverted, build clean, clippy 0 warnings; only the diagnostics (`src/stage2/invariants.rs`, the `--viz-seeds` flags, `tools/invariants.sh`, `tools/inv_analyze.py`) plus your two doc edits remain modified. Nothing committed.

The cone is **not** the torus problem. Same symptom, different cause — and the mechanism is worth being precise about.

## What happens to your facet 85

`ConicalSurface::fit_surface` returned a **cylinder**, not a cone. Half-angle 0, radius 8.76, on a surface whose true half-angle is 9.46° — hence 222× vtol on its own six vertices. The cone rung was attempted and thrown away.

Tallying why, over the cone-rung refusals on `simple_cone`:

| refusals | reason |
|---|---|
| 11 (42%) | `axis_normals_consistent` rejects the fitted axis (`NORMAL_AXIS_TOL`) |
| 7 (27%) | fitted half-angle outside `[2°, 85°]` |
| 5 (19%) | `fit_cone` returned `None` |
| 3 (12%) | apex 429 / 429 / 2128 mm away on a 41 mm model, over `10 × bb_diag` |

Then, with the cone gone, the fallback cylinder is whatever it is: radii of 10.12, 9.51, 8.00, 7.39, 8.23, 7.92, **1538.65**, 5.94, **969.68** — the last two being near-planar cylinders on a 10 mm cone.

So the guards are doing their job. The cone fit really is producing garbage from a 6-vertex chain, and the garbage really should be refused.

## Why it's garbage, and why this differs from the torus

One of the fitted cones was **half-angle 72.85° (true 9.46°), axis 79.7° off, apex 10.8 patch-extents away — fitting the six vertices to 6.66e-16 mm, sse 1.245e-30.** That is *better than the truth*, which only reaches 3.29e-7 because the mesh itself is only float32-exact. My tool now says so outright:

> VERDICT: NOT IDENTIFIABLE — the fitted cone explains these 6 vertices 1.7e17× BETTER than the true one. A second exact cone passes through them; no optimizer can prefer the truth.

The arithmetic behind it: a cone has **6 DOF** (apex 3 + axis 2 + half-angle 1) and your chain rule supplies **exactly 6 vertices**. An exactly-determined nonlinear system has several roots, and nothing in the residual distinguishes them. The torus case was the opposite — there the truth beat the fitted surface by 1.4e7×, so the minimum was at the truth and only the *starting point* was wrong, which is why fixing the initialization worked.

Over the three cone models the split is **8 CONVERGENCE / 1 NOT IDENTIFIABLE**, so most cone failures are still in principle fixable — but they fail through the guards rather than around them, and the guards are correct.

## A third mode the tool had been mislabelling

Several cone seeds reported "SEED REJECTED — the seed set's own fit refuses its own facets" while simultaneously showing `own fit: vertex 0.00x vtol`. That contradiction was mine: `grow_clean` returns `SeedRejected` whenever the flood comes back empty on *any* round, and I was always describing it as round 0. It now distinguishes them:

> REFIT DRIFTED OFF ITS OWN SEED after 1 round — the seed's own fit was fine; the fit of the grown support no longer validates the seed

That's the fixpoint iteration diverging: the seed fits itself at 0.00× vtol, growth admits some facets, the refit on the larger support moves far enough that the seed no longer validates (blocked at 399–1455× vtol), and everything collapses. Distinct from a bad seed, and distinct from non-identifiability.

## Current cone numbers

| model | cone anchors with a working seed |
|---|---|
| `nosecone` | 10/12 (83.3%) |
| `cone_cylinder` | 7/12 (58.3%) |
| `simple_cone` | 4/12 (33.3%) |

Unchanged by the torus fixes, as expected — different fitter.

## What I'd conclude for the seed rule

Your cylinder rule works at 6 vertices because a cylinder is 5 DOF against 6 constraints — one redundant, enough to pin the right root. **A cone at 6 vertices has zero redundancy**, and that is the whole difference. The `apex3` alternative doesn't help here either: it also gives an exactly-determined system.

So the cone rule needs *margin*, not a different shape — enough vertices that only the true cone fits. My earlier support-size curve puts the crossover high: cone axis error median 45.7° at 2 facets, 34.3° at 4, 2.59° at 12, 0.034° at 64. That is consistent with what you're seeing and suggests the cone genuinely cannot be seeded from a chain at all, which is why I'd reach it by promotion from a validated cylinder rather than by its own seed rule.

I have not tried to fix the cone fitter. Say the word if you want me to — the 8-of-9 convergence share says there is something to get, most likely in whatever `fit_cone` uses for its initial apex, given the 429–2128 mm runaways.

```bash
/// cylinder stalls, try to promote the accumulated support to a cone.
///
/// This exists because the two developable types fail in opposite ways at seed
/// scale, measured:
///
/// - A cylinder is 5 DOF against the 6 vertices the section's chain rule
///   supplies — one redundant constraint, enough to pin the right root. 94% of
///   cylinder facets have a working seed set.
/// - A cone is 6 DOF against the same 6 vertices — *zero* redundancy. An
///   exactly-determined nonlinear system has several roots and the residual
///   cannot tell them apart: on `simple_cone` the fitter found a half-angle
///   72.85° cone (true 9.46°) with its apex 10.8 patch-extents away that
///   explains the six vertices to 6.7e-16 mm, better than the true cone
///   manages against a float32 mesh. Of the cone rung's refusals, 42% are
///   `axis_normals_consistent`, 27% a half-angle outside [2°, 85°], 12% an apex
///   429–2128 mm from a 41 mm model — the guards catching real garbage — and
///   what is then left is the fallback cylinder, up to 234x vertex tolerance out.
///
/// So a cone should not be seeded. It should be *reached*: seed the thing that
/// is over-determined, grow it until it cannot go further, and only then fit the
/// 6-DOF surface, on a support large enough to have redundancy. The stall is
/// also informative rather than incidental — a cylinder on a cone stalls after a
/// row or two because the radius diverges linearly along the ruling, so the
/// stalled frontier is exactly where the cone signal is strongest.
///
/// Same shape as stage 2.3(c)'s `promote_bend` (cylinder → torus for bent
/// tubes), which is the precedent for this working.
fn grow_promote_cone(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    in_region: &[bool],
    seed: &[usize],
    centroids: &[[f64; 3]],
    config: &Config,
) -> (Basin, Vec<usize>, usize, bool, Option<super::conical::ConeFit>, bool) {
    let vtol = config.vertex_tolerance_mm;
    let stol = config.surface_tolerance_mm;
    let mut cur: Vec<usize> = seed.to_vec();
    cur.sort_unstable();
    let mut self_ok = false;
    let mut promoted = false;
    let mut fit_out: Option<super::conical::ConeFit> = None;

    // Flood the union of the components containing any seed member.
    let flood_all = |fit: &super::conical::ConeFit| -> Vec<usize> {
        let mut next: HashSet<usize> = HashSet::new();
        for &st in seed {
            if next.contains(&st) {
                continue;
            }
            next.extend(compete::flood::<ConicalSurface>(
                mesh, in_region, st, fit, centroids, vtol, stol,
            ));
        }
        let mut v: Vec<usize> = next.into_iter().collect();
        v.sort_unstable();
        v
    };

    for round in 0..MAX_CLEAN_ROUNDS {
        let verts = vertices_of(mesh, &cur);

        // --- the CYLINDER rung, on its own ---
        let cyl = super::cylindrical::fit_cylinder(&cur, &verts, &mesh.faces, &mesh.vertices)
            .filter(|(_, dir, _)| {
                super::conical::axis_normals_consistent(&cur, &mesh.faces, dir, 0.0)
            })
            .map(|(origin, dir, radius)| {
                let mut f = super::conical::ConeFit {
                    apex: origin,
                    axis_direction: dir,
                    half_angle: 0.0,
                    radius,
                    convex: None,
                };
                ConicalSurface::determine_convexity(mesh, &cur, &mut f);
                f
            });

        // --- the CONE rung, attempted only once the support is grown ---
        // `MIN_CONE_PROMOTION_FACES` is not a tolerance: it is the point at
        // which a 6-DOF fit has any redundancy at all. Six vertices is exact,
        // so the bar is stated in vertices, and 10 leaves four spare.
        const MIN_CONE_PROMOTION_VERTS: usize = 10;
        let cone = if verts.len() >= MIN_CONE_PROMOTION_VERTS {
            super::conical::fit_cone(&cur, &verts, &mesh.faces, &mesh.vertices).and_then(
                |(apex, dir, ha)| {
                    let deg = ha.to_degrees();
                    if !(super::conical::MIN_HALF_ANGLE_DEG
                        ..=super::conical::MAX_HALF_ANGLE_DEG)
                        .contains(&deg)
                        || !super::conical::axis_normals_consistent(&cur, &mesh.faces, &dir, ha)
                    {
                        return None;
                    }
                    let mut f = super::conical::ConeFit {
                        apex,
                        axis_direction: dir,
                        half_angle: ha,
                        radius: 0.0,
                        convex: None,
                    };
                    ConicalSurface::determine_convexity(mesh, &cur, &mut f);
                    Some(f)
                },
            )
        } else {
            None
        };

        // Grow with each rung and keep whichever reaches further. Area, not
        // residual: residual on the current support is what cannot tell a cone
        // from its impostors, and the whole point of promoting is that the cone
        // should be able to go somewhere the cylinder cannot.
        let mut best: Option<(Vec<usize>, super::conical::ConeFit, bool)> = None;
        for (f, is_cone) in [(cyl, false), (cone, true)].into_iter() {
            let Some(f) = f else { continue };
            let grown = flood_all(&f);
            if grown.is_empty() {
                continue;
            }
            let better = match &best {
                None => true,
                Some((g, _, _)) => grown.len() > g.len(),
            };
            if better {
                best = Some((grown, f, is_cone));
            }
        }

        let Some((grown, f, is_cone)) = best else {
            return (
                if round == 0 {
                    Basin::NoFit
                } else {
                    Basin::SeedRejected
                },
                cur,
                round,
                self_ok,
                fit_out,
                promoted,
            );
        };
        if round == 0 {
            self_ok = seed.iter().all(|&fi| {
                compete::face_validates::<ConicalSurface>(mesh, fi, &f, centroids, vtol, stol)
            });
        }
        promoted |= is_cone;
        fit_out = Some(f);
        if grown == cur {
            return (Basin::Exact, cur, round, self_ok, fit_out, promoted);
        }
        cur = grown;
    }
    (
        Basin::NoConverge,
        cur,
        MAX_CLEAN_ROUNDS,
        self_ok,
        fit_out,
        promoted,
    )
}

/// Classify a converged result against the reference face.'''
```

```bash
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,

) -> SeedCase {

        mesh, in_region, seed, truth, centroids, config, shape, ref_surf, verdict, result, rounds,

}
```

> Actually, I think I found it. The `axis_normals_consistent` check with a half-angle of 0 requires normals to be perpendicular to the cylinder axis, but on a cone with a 9.46° half-angle, the facet normals aren't perpendicular — they're at about 0.164 relative to the axis. This check is killing the cylinder fit on round 0, making `cyl` None, which cascades to `best` being None and returning NoFit immediately. That's exactly why I'm seeing 0/12 with no promotion happening at all.
> 
> The real issue is that I'm applying this perpendicularity filter too strictly in the promotion path. The cylinder is meant to be a stepping stone on cone data where it's knowingly approximate — the filter should only guard whether to *commit* a cylinder as a final result, not whether to use it as an initializer. I need to remove that filter from the promotion path and retest, plus add some debug output to see what's actually happening if it still fails. I should also clean up those unused variable warnings in the diagnose function while I'm at it.

## 🤖 Assistant
<!-- msg_011Cdmj8AxidKwtEcSLtb4pP -->

I implemented it and it works on the pure cone — but the mechanism is not the one either of us expected, and the measurement says so plainly.

## Cylinder → cone is refuted

The obvious design fails at the first step: **a cylinder fitted to cone data grows by nothing.** `cyl grows to 3` from a 3-facet support, 4 from 4, 2 from 2 — on all 36 cone anchors, promotion fired 0 times. On a 9.46° cone the radius diverges along every ruling, so at vtol = 5e-5 mm a cylinder is wrong immediately and there is no straight stretch to accumulate on.

`promote_bend` gets away with a cylinder because a bend genuinely *is* locally a cylinder — DEVELOPMENT_PLAN records the sag as ~3.6e-5 mm over a 2 mm patch at R = 14, inside tolerance. A cone offers no such stretch. That asymmetry is the whole reason the analogy doesn't carry.

(One thing I got wrong on the way and had to measure out: I first filtered the cylinder rung with `axis_normals_consistent(..., half_angle = 0)`, which demands normals perpendicular to the axis. On a cone they sit at `|n·d| = sin α`, so that guard rejects every cylinder fitted to cone data by construction. Removing it changed nothing — the cylinder still didn't grow.)

## Plane → cone doesn't fire either

Phase 1.2's measured fact — a cone's tangent plane is constant along a ruling, so a plane explains its neighbours up that ruling to ~5e-7 mm — made a plane the natural stepping stone: a ruling is exactly what pins a cone, since all rulings meet at the apex. Implemented, the plane rung reaches **0 facets on every round of every anchor**. The exact-along-a-ruling result evidently doesn't survive the plane fit plus centroid and orientation clauses at this tolerance.

## What actually worked is support enlargement

The trace tells the story:

```
round 0: support   3 facets /   5 verts | plane reaches 0 | cone none
round 3: support  27 facets /  33 verts | plane reaches 0 | cone none
round 7: support 137 facets / 118 verts | plane reaches 0 | cone grows to 212  ← identifiable
round 8: support 212 facets / 176 verts |                 | cone grows to 212  ← fixpoint
```

Every step from 3 to 137 is the bounded one-ring expansion I added as a fallback. No promotion, no stepping stone — just enlarging the support until the 6-DOF cone becomes identifiable, at which point it immediately floods to all 212 facets and converges. The threshold is variable: one anchor needed **118 vertices**, another only 22.

| model | direct fit | with support enlargement |
|---|---|---|
| `simple_cone` | 4/12 (33%) | **12/12 (100%)** |
| `cone_cylinder` | 7/12 (58%) | 6/12 (50%) |
| `nosecone` | 10/12 (83%) | 8/12 (67%) |

So this is the same conclusion the torus ball-ladder reached — *grow the seed until it is admissible* — and it is not "promotion" in the `promote_bend` sense at all.

## Why it regresses the two tangent models

The nosecone failures are all one thing: **`REFIT DRIFTED OFF ITS OWN SEED after 27 rounds`**, with the support having swollen to **646 facets against a 186-facet reference cone**. Ring expansion is undirected, so it walks straight across the cone–sphere tangency, and once the support is 3.5× the true face the cone fit is fitting mostly sphere. The seed's own fit was fine at 0.00× vtol every time; the growth destroyed it.

That's the boundary problem again, and it's the thing ring expansion cannot solve on its own: it needs to stop at the true surface, and on a tangent junction there is nothing local telling it to. `simple_cone`'s cone is bounded by a sharp edge, so expansion is cordoned and reaches 100%; `nosecone`'s and `cone_cylinder`'s are bounded by tangencies, so it runs away.

## Where I'd take it

The honest reading is that a cone needs both halves: enough support to be identifiable (measured: tens of vertices, not six) *and* a bound on where the support may grow. The one bound that is measured-exact in this codebase is the sharp partition, which is precisely what you had me disable — and on `simple_cone`, where it happens to cordon the cone anyway, the result is 100%.

So the next thing worth trying is enlarging the support **only within the smooth region** (or, in the new design, only within whatever replaces it), rather than over the whole mesh. That would keep `simple_cone` at 100% and stop the nosecone runaway. I haven't tried it — say the word.

Everything is behind `--viz-seeds`; `BREPPER_INV_NO_PROMOTE=1` restores the direct cone fit and `BREPPER_INV_PROMOTE_DEBUG=1` prints the per-round trace above. Build clean; I haven't re-run the suite, per your instruction.

```
/// Fit a cone to a support: apex, axis direction, half-angle.
///
/// Exposed so \`super::invariants\` can drive a cylinder-then-cone promotion
/// without going through \`ConicalSurface::fit_surface\`, which chooses between
/// the two rungs internally. Measured, the cone rung is worthless at seed scale
/// and good on a grown support, so a promoting grower needs the two separately.
pub(super) fn fit_cone(
    face_indices: &[usize],
    vertex_set: &[usize],
    faces: &[MeshFace],
    vertices: &[MeshVertex],
) -> Option<([f64; 3], [f64; 3], f64)> {
    if vertex_set.len() < 4 {
        return None;
    }
    let max_err = |fit: &([f64; 3], [f64; 3], f64)| -> f64 {
        vertex_set
            .iter()
            .map(|&vi| vertex_to_cone_distance(&vertices[vi], &fit.0, &fit.1, fit.2).abs())
            .fold(0.0_f64, f64::max)
    };

    // (apex, axis direction, half-angle) with its max vertex error.
    type ScoredConeFit = (f64, ([f64; 3], [f64; 3], f64));
    let primary = fit_cone_primary(face_indices, vertex_set, faces, vertices);
    let mut best: Option<ScoredConeFit> = None;
    if let Some(fit) = primary {
        best = Some((max_err(&fit), fit));
    }

    // Normal-line axis rescue for narrow azimuthal arcs: the primary axis
    // estimates (normal covariance, normal differences) degenerate when the
    // seed's normals are nearly parallel (e.g. side cone patches of a
    // transition piece spanning only a few tessellation columns). Cone
    // surface normals all pass through the axis, so closest-approach
    // midpoints of normal-line pairs trace the axis directly.
    const RESCUE_ERR_THRESHOLD: f64 = 1e-4; // mm
    if best.as_ref().is_none_or(|(e, _)| *e > RESCUE_ERR_THRESHOLD) {
        if let Some(fit) = fit_cone_normal_line_rescue(face_indices, vertex_set, faces, vertices) {
            let err = max_err(&fit);
            if best.as_ref().is_none_or(|(e, _)| err < *e) {
                best = Some((err, fit));
            }
        }
    }

    best.map(|(_, f)| f)
}

/// Closest-approach midpoint between two 3D lines (p1 + t·d1, p2 + s·d2).
/// Returns None for near-parallel lines or when the gap between the closest
/// points is large relative to their distance from the line origins.
fn line_closest_midpoint(
    p1: &[f64; 3],
    d1: &[f64; 3],
    p2: &[f64; 3],
    d2: &[f64; 3],
) -> Option<[f64; 3]> {
    let r = [p2[0] - p1[0], p2[1] - p1[1], p2[2] - p1[2]];
    let a = dot3(d1, d1);
    let b = dot3(d1, d2);
    let c = dot3(d2, d2);
    let d = dot3(d1, &r);
    let e = dot3(d2, &r);
    let denom = a * c - b * b;
    if denom.abs() < 1e-6 {
        return None; // near-parallel
    }
    let t = (d * c - e * b) / denom;
    let sv = (d * b - e * a) / denom;
    let q1 = [p1[0] + t * d1[0], p1[1] + t * d1[1], p1[2] + t * d1[2]];
    let q2 = [p2[0] + sv * d2[0], p2[1] + sv * d2[1], p2[2] + sv * d2[2]];
    let gap = ((q1[0] - q2[0]).powi(2) + (q1[1] - q2[1]).powi(2) + (q1[2] - q2[2]).powi(2)).sqrt();
    let scale = t.abs().max(sv.abs()).max(1e-9);
    if gap > scale * 0.5 {
        return None; // lines don't come close: not a surface of revolution
    }
    Some([
        (q1[0] + q2[0]) / 2.0,
        (q1[1] + q2[1]) / 2.0,
        (q1[2] + q2[2]) / 2.0,
    ])
}
```

```
fn fit_cone_primary(
    face_indices: &[usize],
    vertex_set: &[usize],
    faces: &[MeshFace],
    vertices: &[MeshVertex],
) -> Option<([f64; 3], [f64; 3], f64)> {
    if vertex_set.len() < 4 {
        return None;
    }

    // Check for pointed cone: a vertex present in ALL seed faces.
    let shared_apex = find_shared_apex_vertex(face_indices, faces, vertices);

    // Recenter vertices around their centroid for numerical stability.
    let n_pts = vertex_set.len() as f64;
    let mut centroid = [0.0_f64; 3];
    for &vi in vertex_set.iter() {
        centroid[0] += vertices[vi].x;
        centroid[1] += vertices[vi].y;
        centroid[2] += vertices[vi].z;
    }
    centroid[0] /= n_pts;
    centroid[1] /= n_pts;
    centroid[2] /= n_pts;

    let centered_points: Vec<[f64; 3]> = vertex_set.iter()
        .map(|&vi| [
            vertices[vi].x - centroid[0],
            vertices[vi].y - centroid[1],
            vertices[vi].z - centroid[2],
        ])
        .collect();

    if let Some(apex) = shared_apex {
        // --- Pointed cone path ---
        // For fixed-apex LM, recenter both points and apex.
        let centered_apex = [
            apex[0] - centroid[0],
            apex[1] - centroid[1],
            apex[2] - centroid[2],
        ];
        let mut axis = estimate_axis_from_normal_diffs(face_indices, faces)
            .or_else(|| estimate_axis_from_apex(&apex, vertex_set, vertices))?;
        let half_angle = estimate_half_angle(&apex, &mut axis, vertex_set, vertices)?;

        let problem = ConeFixedApexLMProblem::new(centered_points, centered_apex, axis, half_angle);
        let (result, _report) = LevenbergMarquardt::new().with_patience(150).minimize(problem);
        let refined_dir = result.axis_dir_from_params(&result.params);
        let refined_ha = result.params[2];
        if refined_ha > 0.01 && refined_ha < 85.0_f64.to_radians() {
            Some((apex, refined_dir, refined_ha))
        } else {
            Some((apex, axis, half_angle))
        }
    } else {
        // --- Truncated cone path ---
        // Multi-strategy axis: covariance for ≥8 faces, vertex-based for seeds
        let mut axis = compute_truncated_cone_axis(
            face_indices, vertex_set, faces, vertices)?;

        // Step 2+3: Apex and half-angle from linear regression of vertex projections.
        let (apex, half_angle) = estimate_apex_and_angle_from_profile(
            &mut axis, vertex_set, vertices)?;

        // Full LM refinement with recentered coordinates
        let centered_apex = [
            apex[0] - centroid[0],
            apex[1] - centroid[1],
            apex[2] - centroid[2],
        ];
        let problem = ConeLMProblem::new(centered_points, axis, centered_apex, half_angle);
        let (result, _report) = LevenbergMarquardt::new().with_patience(150).minimize(problem);
        let refined_dir = result.axis_dir_from_params(&result.params);
        let refined_apex = [
            result.params[2] + centroid[0],
            result.params[3] + centroid[1],
            result.params[4] + centroid[2],
        ];
```

```
pub(crate) fn cone(faces: &[usize], mesh: &ConnectedMesh, vtol: f64) -> Option<Initial> {

/// The taper solve itself: axis from the centred normals, half-angle from the
/// normals, and only the position from a linear least squares.
///
/// # Why not (apex, axis, half-angle)
///
/// Phase 1.2 measured the cost of estimating the apex directly: on three
/// adjacent facets of an 18.4° cone the plane-concurrence solve returned a
/// half-angle of 87° with the apex halfway up the model, and the fit then
/// validated none of the three facets it was built from. The apex runs off to
/// **infinity** as a patch flattens toward a cylinder, and an estimator for an
/// unbounded quantity explodes near its degenerate case.
///
/// So both shape parameters come from quantities that stay bounded and local,
/// and neither is derived from the apex:
///
/// * the **axis direction**, exactly, from the centred normal covariance;
/// * the **taper** \`sin α = |n·d|\`, averaged over the facets — a nearly

///   short the patch is. (It carries the \`O(Δθ²/8)\` chord-plane bias Phase 1.1
///   measured — 1.5e-3 relative at Δθ = 0.11 rad — which is a rounding error

///
/// Only the *position* then needs solving, and it is a plain linear least
/// squares. Writing \`u\` for the axis offset from the patch centroid within the
/// plane perpendicular to \`d\`, \`z_A\` for the apex's axial coordinate, and
/// \`m = |u|² − tan²α · z_A²\`, the surface condition
/// \`|r − u|² = tan²α (z − z_A)²\` rearranges to
///
/// \`\`\`text
///   |r|² − tan²α z² = 2 r·u − 2 tan²α z · z_A − m
/// \`\`\`
///
/// which is linear in \`(u₁, u₂, z_A, m)\`. Least squares then returns whatever
/// best explains the support, so the fit **interpolates its own facets** rather
/// than extrapolating to a far-off point — that is what makes it degrade
/// gracefully. On a short patch \`z_A\` is uncertain, but the residuals on the
/// data stay small, so validation passes and the patch keeps growing; as the
/// patch lengthens \`z_A\` sharpens and the cone emerges on its own.
///
/// \`taper = 0\` is a **cylinder**, a finite value in the middle of the parameter
/// range rather than \`apex = ∞\` at its edge — the same reason circle fitters
/// use \`κ = 1/r\`. A patch whose whole radius change hides inside \`vtol\` cannot
/// distinguish the two, and this returns the cylinder in that case. That test
/// is derived from the tolerance and the patch's own extent; it adds no
/// constant.
fn cone_tapered(faces: &[usize], mesh: &ConnectedMesh, vtol: f64) -> Option<Initial> {
    let mut axis = cone_axis_from_centred_normals(faces, mesh)?;

    // sin α from the normals: constant on a cone, so an average is stable at
    // any patch size, and it never touches a position.
    let mut sin_sum = 0.0;
    let mut count = 0_usize;
    for &fi in faces {
        if let Some(n) = mesh.faces[fi].normal {
            sin_sum += dot3(&n, &axis).abs();
            count += 1;
        }
    }
    if count == 0 {
        return None;
    }
    let sin_alpha = (sin_sum / count as f64).clamp(0.0, 1.0);
    let cos_alpha = (1.0 - sin_alpha * sin_alpha).max(0.0).sqrt();
    if cos_alpha <= MIN_CROSS_NORM {
        return None; // a plane, not a cone
    }
    let tan_alpha = sin_alpha / cos_alpha;

    let verts = patch_vertices(faces, mesh);
    if verts.len() < 4 {
        return None;
    }
    let inv = 1.0 / verts.len() as f64;
    let mut origin = [0.0_f64; 3];
    for &vi in &verts {
        let v = &mesh.vertices[vi];
        origin = add(origin, scale([v.x, v.y, v.z], inv));
    }
    let (e1, e2) = perpendicular_basis(&axis);
```

```
4.1     Kinematic Field Fitting
Kinematic surface fitting is a type of fitting procedure aimed at reconstructing shapes that can be
generated by sweeping a general profile curve along a simple, linear velocity field, such as surfaces of
revolution [5]. These methods work by reconstructing velocity fields, and can be adapted for quadric
fitting to find properties of the desired quadric: the axis of invariance for a cylinder, or the axis of
rotation for a spheroid, or the central point of scaling for a general cone. We can use that property to
transform the data to a space where the type-specific quadric fitting problem is easier to specify.
     Kinematic velocity fields are linear functions v(p) that define a velocity everywhere in space. For
our quadric fitting catalog we use three specific field types (Fig. 7): First, the simple general cylinder
field due to [20], which defines a constant velocity field: v(p) = a , where a is a parameter vector
defining the direction of the field. Second, we use the rotational field due to [18], which defines a
rotational (or helical) motion: v(p) = r×p + a , where r and a are parameter vectors encoding the
rotation axis and position of the axis (plus helical motion, if any). And finally, we use a scaling field,

4.3     Fitting General Cones
To fit a cone, we first find the center point of scaling by fitting the kinematic scaling field
v(p) = γ p + a . The center of scaling is −a / γ . Note that if γ is very small, then division by γ becomes
unstable. In the limit, as γ → 0 , the center of scaling moves infinitely far from the origin, so the cone
becomes a cylinder. We therefore define a threshold tcyl = 10−6 , and if γ < t cyl , we consider the best
cone to be a cylinder, so we can fit an elliptical cylinder instead of a cone (see Sec. 4.2). Alternatively, if
a cylinder is not desired, we can take the best eigenvector returned by algebraic fitting with γ > t cyl .
      Once some (non-infinite) cone center is chosen, we can translate the points so that the cone center
is at the origin, and fit a centered cone quadric equation c4 px2 + c5 py2 + c6 pz2 + c7 px py + c8 px pz + c9 py pz = 0
using Taubin’s method. Finally, we translate the resulting quadric back to the original space.

4.4     Fitting Rotationally Symmetric Quadrics
To fit a rotationally symmetric quadric, we first find the axis of rotational symmetry by fitting the
rotational field v(p) = r×p + a . We normalize the resulting parameters by dividing both a and r by
 r , and then find a point on the axis of the rotational field pr = r × (a − (a·r)r) . If r is very small, then

normalizing by r        is unstable, so we use a threshold tcyl = 10−6 : If r < t cyl then we assume r ≈ 0 so
the best motion is approximately a pure translation, i.e. a cylinder; we then fit a circular cylinder (see
Sec. 4.2). Otherwise, we transform the data so that the z-axis is aligned with r , and the point pr is at

the origin. We then fit the equation c0 + c3 pz + c4 (px2 + py2 ) + c6 pz2 = 0 for a general quadric with rotational
symmetry, and finally transform the result back to the original basis. We can directly apply the
methods of Section 3 to further constrain the quadric type.
   For circular cones we either find the center of scaling and make that pr , then fit the simpler
equation c4 (px2 + py2 ) + c6pz2 = 0 , or we can alternatively rotate the data points to a shared plane and fit a
2D line to find the angle of the cone. Note that quadric cones are in fact two cones connected at the
tip, and this second method ignores the possibility that the data points may come from both cones;
but it may be desirable in the common case where only one of the two cones is desired in the fit.
      For spheres we directly fit the equation c0 + c1px + c2 py + c3 pz + c4 (px2 + py2 + pz2 ) = 0 [2]. For planes, we

translate the data to its centroid and fit the equation c1px + c2 py + c3 pz = 0 [16]. We handle double
planes and intersecting planes with multiple plane fits, because we prefer single-plane solutions.
```

Searched, and the literature answers your preference directly — with a negative.

## Your preferred shape does not exist

Andrews & Séquin state it flatly: **"there is no known linear least-squares method to fit circular cones and cylinders to a point cloud"** using point positions alone, citing Petitjean's survey. They contrast that with normals, for which linear methods do exist (Lukács–Martin–Marshall). The reason matches what I derived before searching: a right circular cone is a quadric whose 3×3 form must be `M = ddᵀ − cos²α·I`, i.e. **must have a repeated eigenvalue** — and that condition is not linear or even quadratic in the quadric coefficients, so it can't be imposed on a linear fit.

So "analytic, ≥6 points, points only, no ruling structure" is asking for something that isn't known to exist. Two things nearby *do*.

## The one I'd actually build — and your codebase already has half of it

Andrews & Séquin get the cone apex from a **kinematic scaling field** `v(p) = γp + a`, fitted by requiring the field be tangent to the surface, `v(p)·n(p) = 0`. Written out, each oriented facet contributes one linear equation:

```
γ (p·n) + a·n = 0
```

Four unknowns, homogeneous, so a null-space solve from **3 facets**. The apex is `A = −a/γ`.

Now divide through by γ: `n·(p − A) = 0`. **That is exactly Phase 1.1's `nᵢ·A = nᵢ·pᵢ`** — the relation already in `initialize.rs`. The literature's version is the same geometry in a different parameterization, and the difference is the whole point. `initialize::cone`'s doc comment explains why the apex solve was rejected:

> the apex runs off to **infinity** as a patch flattens toward a cylinder, and an estimator for an unbounded quantity explodes near its degenerate case

In `(γ, a)` coordinates that objection dissolves: **γ → 0 *is* the cylinder**, a regular interior point of the parameter space, and the paper's treatment is literally "if γ is below a floor, fit a cylinder instead". This is the same Pratt/Taubin move your DEVELOPMENT_PLAN already praises for the bent tube (`k = 1/R`, "no infinity anywhere") — applied to the cone apex rather than the spine curvature. Phase 1.1 rejected the right relation for a reason that the right parameterization removes.

The full pipeline, all closed-form, no iteration:

| step | solve | needs |
|---|---|---|
| apex | null space of rows `[p·n, nₓ, n_y, n_z]` | **3 facets** |
| axis + half-angle | translate apex to origin, fit `Σcᵢⱼ pᵢpⱼ = 0` (Taubin), then eigendecompose `M` | **5 points** |

`M`'s eigenvalues are `(sin²α, −cos²α, −cos²α)`: the odd one out gives the axis, and `tan²α = λ_single / −λ_repeated`. No ring structure, no ruling alignment needed for the *algebra* — the plane relation is exact for a facet spanning two rulings and carries only the `O(Δθ²/8)` chord-plane lean otherwise, which Phase 1.1 measured at 1.5e-3 relative. Ample for an initializer.

The honest limit: it needs **3 facets, not 2**. Your facet-85 seed has 2 quads → 2 normals, and no normals-based method can work from 2. That's structural, not a defect.

## The points-only option, if you insist on no normals

Fit an unconstrained general quadric — linear, 10 coefficients, 9 DOF, so **≥9 points** — then project `M` onto the circular-cone form by averaging its two closest eigenvalues. Fully analytic, points only, no ruling structure. It's biased (algebraic not geometric distance) so it's an initializer, not an answer. Point count is reachable at modest support: a 4-quad vertex star has 9 vertices, a 4-quad chain has 10. Your 2-quad, 6-vertex seed is out.

## Considered and rejected

- **Solving the 6-DOF system from exactly 6 points.** Exactly determined, so finitely many right circular cones pass through them — but it's a polynomial system with multiple roots and no least-squares character. It is also precisely the configuration where I measured a *second exact cone* (half-angle 72.85°) fitting to 6.7e-16. Six points genuinely admit more than one cone; the two-circle construction escapes that only because the ring structure supplies extra information.
- **Orthogonal-distance geometric fitting** (Lukács et al.; Ahn's LNCS 3151). This is the right *refinement*, and it's what your LM already is. It doesn't solve initialization.

## One thing worth checking before any of this

Reading `compute_truncated_cone_axis` ([conical.rs:89](src/stage2/conical.rs:89)) again: with fewer than 8 faces it tries strategy 2 — a vertex shared by "most" faces, axis = that vertex to the centroid of the others — and **returns as soon as any candidate yields a normalizable direction**. Strategy 3 below it, `estimate_axis_from_normal_diffs`, is exact on a cone (`(nᵢ − nⱼ)·d = 0`, so the cross product of two independent differences *is* the axis) and needs only 3 normals. It is unreachable whenever strategy 2 fires — and with 2 faces the threshold is `2.max(2) − 1 = 1`, so *every* vertex qualifies and strategy 2 always fires.

So on small supports an exact method is being shadowed by a placeholder guess. That is very likely the whole story behind the 2.54° half-angle, it costs nothing to test, and it would tell you how much of the cone problem is a fitter defect versus a real information limit before you build anything new. ///
```
/// Strategy 1 (≥8 faces): covariance smallest-eigenvector.
/// Strategy 2 (few faces, shared vertex): apex→base-centroid direction.
/// Strategy 3 (few faces, no shared vertex): cross product of normal diffs.
fn compute_truncated_cone_axis(
    face_indices: &[usize],
    vertex_set: &[usize],
    faces: &[MeshFace],
    vertices: &[MeshVertex],
) -> Option<[f64; 3]> {
    // With many faces, covariance is robust.
    if face_indices.len() >= 8 {
        return estimate_axis_from_normals(face_indices, faces, vertices);
    }

    // Strategy 2: vertex shared by most faces → axis from that vertex to centroid.
    let mut vertex_face_count = std::collections::HashMap::<usize, usize>::new();
    for &fi in face_indices {
        let vc = faces[fi].vertex_count as usize;
        for &vi in &faces[fi].vertex_indices[..vc] {
            *vertex_face_count.entry(vi).or_insert(0) += 1;
        }
    }
    let threshold = face_indices.len().max(2) - 1;
    let mut apex_candidates: Vec<usize> = vertex_face_count.iter()
        .filter(|(_, &c)| c >= threshold)
        .map(|(&vi, _)| vi)
        .collect();
    apex_candidates.sort(); // deterministic

    for &apex_vi in &apex_candidates {
        let other_verts: Vec<usize> = vertex_set.iter()
            .filter(|&&vi| vi != apex_vi)
            .copied()
            .collect();
        if other_verts.is_empty() { continue; }
        let mut bx = 0.0_f64;
        let mut by = 0.0_f64;
        let mut bz = 0.0_f64;
        for &vi in &other_verts {
            bx += vertices[vi].x;
            by += vertices[vi].y;
            bz += vertices[vi].z;
        }
        let n = other_verts.len() as f64;
        bx /= n; by /= n; bz /= n;
        let mut axis = [
            bx - vertices[apex_vi].x,
            by - vertices[apex_vi].y,
            bz - vertices[apex_vi].z,
        ];
        let len = normalize3(&mut axis);
        if len > 1e-10 {
            return Some(axis);
        }
    }

    // Strategy 3: cross product of normal differences.
    estimate_axis_from_normal_diffs(face_indices, faces)
}
```
</details>
